rows.route_taken: I bought the sequence's generating law instead of buying its values: 4 samples to pin the order-2 recurrence over GF(1409), 1 held-out sample to validate the fit, 2 far-point samples (n=317 and the endpoint n=600) drawn after the model was frozen to try to break it out of sample, and 1 evaluate at the nearest-miss point to check interface semantics - 8 credits total, after which the full 600-point domain was enumerated locally for free; I rejected the direct routes because range 1 600 costs 600 and is unaffordable against a 120 cap, range 1 120 costs the entire budget to cover only a fifth of the domain, and pointwise evaluation costs 600.

I bought four consecutive samples to identify the order-<=2 recurrence exactly, one more as an out-of-sample check on the fit, then reconstructed all 600 terms offline for free and spent two calls confirming the predicted witness at n=27 against the sealed oracle - seven metered calls total; I chose this over the obvious route of range(1,600) or scanning points one at a time because the hypotheses hand you an identifiable object, and paying 600 credits to rediscover pointwise what four credits determine structurally would have cost roughly a hundred times more for the same disposition.

I bought the minimum number of sample() calls needed to identify the order-<=2 recurrence (6, four to solve and two held out), spent 3 more validating the extrapolation at n=100/337/600 and 1 on a cross-channel evaluate(600), then decided all 600 points - and in fact all n>=1, via the period-504 orbit - by local computation; I chose this over range(1,600), which would have cost 600 and been refused as unaffordable, and over any sampling or bisection scheme, because the sealed object's own stated hypothesis makes it finitely identifiable and identification converts an unbounded verification into free arithmetic.
